cards.front: Recall a key point about Melody
cards.back: Conjunct melody moves by step (adjacent notes); disjunct melody leaps between distant notes — each creates different character.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Melody
cards.back: Triadic melodies outline chord shapes; scalic melodies run up/down scales; arpeggio melodies break chords into individual notes.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Melody
cards.back: Passing notes connect chord notes melodically; ornamental notes (acciaccatura, appoggiatura) decorate the main melody.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Melody
cards.back: Ostinato is a repeated melodic pattern that provides a foundation — used extensively in Baroque, minimalism and popular music.

cards.front: What should you know about music exam tips?
cards.back: Always identify the TYPE of melody using AQA vocabulary. Note any ornamentation by name. Explain how melodic choices create character or mood. Compare melody between sections.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Melody just means the tune — any description of a tune is acceptable. Correct: Melody has specific TYPE vocabulary: conjunct (stepwise), disjunct (leaping), triadic, scalic, arpeggio. Always identify the TYPE of melody and its effect, not just say it is a tune. Examiners reward precise terminology.
Listen to a piece of music and describe its melody using at least four terms from the AQA elements list. Explain how the melodic features contribute to the character of the piece.
AO1 — Knowledge: Show knowledge of Melody using appropriate musical vocabulary (e.g. terminology for elements, devices, and contexts).

Melody is a key element of GCSE Music requiring theoretical understanding and practical application. The AQA specification requires you to identify, describe and analyse this element in set works and unfamiliar music. Focus on the specific AQA terminology — examiners reward precise vocabulary over vague descriptions. Understanding how melody contributes to the overall character and effect of a pie

cards.front: Applying Melody in Performance and Composition
cards.back: Understanding melody informs your performing (AO1) and composing (AO2) work. In performance, awareness of melody helps you make interpretive decisions that serve the music. In composition, melody provides the building blocks of your creative work — the choices you make about this element shape the identity and coherence of your piece.

In the AQA GCSE Music listening exam, questions about melody typically ask you to: identify features by ear; describe how they are used; explain their effect; compare features between extracts. The key to success is precise terminology — never use vague language.
